enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable (cross-sectional qualitative comparative case study with no longitudinal cohort follow-up; interview refusal or non-response rates are not reported).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (comparative analysis of n=3 single-jurisdiction cases cannot isolate regulatory-regime effects from national legal traditions, utility ownership structures or historical civic attitudes, a limitation explicitly noted in the Discussion on PDF p. 10).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (primary statutes, regional decrees, contractual agreements and regulatory procedures in the Netherlands, Catalonia/Barcelona and Scotland are specifically cited and mapped across 15 de jure and de facto governance indicators in Table 3, though ordinal L/M/H thresholds lack formal coding rules).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern (formal legal/regulatory rules are corroborated against statutes and published determinations, but interview questionnaires are unpublished, relative L/M/H coding procedures and inter-rater reliability are unreported, and author/funder ties to Vitens and Suez Environment/Agbar create potential observer bias).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak for service/welfare outcomes, adequate for procedural mapping (the evaluated outcome is comparative presence of procedural consumer-inclusion mechanisms rated L/M/H rather than actual effectiveness of participation or household affordability/service impacts; Table 2 utility indicators are purely descriptive context for 2007 with missing Dutch sanitation data).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concerns / Can't tell (no pre-registered study protocol; the full interview questionnaire and detailed informant data are withheld as available on request in Footnote 1, though narrative reporting candidly discusses countervailing findings such as accountability barriers in Scotland).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (purposive selection of three Western European utilities—Vitens, Agbar and Scottish Water—for analytical generalization; within-case key-informant sample sizes, recruitment procedures and response rates are unreported in the text).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its research objective and hypotheses: to investigate whether and how three economic regulatory regimes for water pricing (self-regulation, bipartite negotiation and independent regulation) incorporate mechanisms for consumer inclusion across transparency, participation and accountability, hypothesizing that self-regulation is least inclusive and independent regulation most inclusive.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 1 of 13] Abstract (p. 459); [PDF Page 2 of 13] Introduction (p. 460); [PDF Page 4 of 13] Research design (p. 462)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative comparative case-study methodology combining key-informant interviews with legal and regulatory documentary analysis is appropriate for investigating formal and informal institutional mechanisms of transparency, stakeholder participation and regulatory accountability in water tariff setting.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify a comparative three-case design (Vitens in the Netherlands, Agbar/EMA in Barcelona and Scottish Water/WICS in Scotland) aimed at analytical rather than statistical generalization, selecting large Western European utilities operating at cost-recovery tariffs to hold broad operational context comparable while varying regulatory regime, and structuring comparison around Stern & Holder's (1999) governance framework.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 4-5 of 13] Research design & Description of the selected cases (pp. 461-463)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Footnote 2 notes only that key informants included respondents from regulators, service providers, public authorities and consumer representative bodies, and Table 2 footnotes mention staff consultations at Vitens, Agbar and WICS; however, the paper does not report the number of interviewees per case, how informants were identified or recruited, selection criteria or non-participation.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 4 of 13] Research design, Footnotes 1-2 (p. 462); [PDF Page 5 of 13] Table 2 footnotes (p. 463)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Although data collection combined interviews using a questionnaire and secondary regulatory/legal documents aligned with Stern & Holder's (1999) governance principles, the paper omits the questionnaire content, interview setting/mode, audio recording or transcription practices, number of interviews conducted and whether data saturation was considered, referring readers to the authors for the questionnaire and interviewee details (Footnote 1).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Reflexivity and potential conflicts of interest are not examined despite direct institutional ties to two of the three studied cases: the first author is affiliated with Vitens Evides International (linked to Dutch case-study utility Vitens), the research was funded by Suez Environment (historically linked to Barcelona case-study operator Agbar) and the Acknowledgements specifically thank an Agbar representative for guidance and contributions, with no discussion of how these relationships affected access, informant candour or comparative scoring.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 1 of 13] Author affiliations (p. 459); [PDF Page 11 of 13] Acknowledgements (p. 469)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper contains no discussion of research ethics review, informed consent procedures or anonymity/confidentiality safeguards for key informants (mentioning confidentiality only in the statutory context of Scottish public consultation submissions and commercial secrets).
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 4 of 13] Research design (p. 462); [PDF Page 9 of 13] Transparency & Participation (pp. 466-467)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While Stern & Holder's (1999) framework provides a clear 15-indicator structure across transparency, participation and accountability (Table 3), the authors do not describe how qualitative interview data were coded, how discrepancies across stakeholder perspectives were reconciled, whether multiple researchers independently assigned the comparative ordinal ratings (L, M, H) or what explicit operational thresholds separated Lowest, Middle and Highest ratings.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 4 of 13] Research design (p. 462); [PDF Pages 7-10 of 13] Application of regulatory governance principles & Table 3 (pp. 465-468)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized by governance principle in Table 3 and accompanying narrative sections, explicitly contrasting formal legal provisions with practical realities (such as consumer representatives holding only 2 of 18 votes on Barcelona's Prices Commission and high transaction-cost barriers to judicial review in Scotland) and relating evidence directly back to the initial hypotheses and limitations.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 7-11 of 13] Application of regulatory governance principles, Table 3, Discussion & Conclusion (pp. 465-469)

domain_ratings.justification: Valuable as a structured comparative institutional analysis illustrating how self-regulation, contract/bipartite negotiation and independent regulation differ in de jure and de facto consumer inclusion in European water tariff setting, while highlighting important distinctions between formal consultation, ex post appeals and informal participation; however, substantive value for causal policy inference is constrained by the small purposive sample (n=3), unassessed downstream effectiveness on tariff/service outcomes and thin reporting of interview methods.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable comparative institutional mapping with clear future research directions, constrained by n=3 purposive design, unmeasured participation effectiveness and limited reporting of primary interview methods.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Pascual Sanz, Schouten and Hantke-Domas (2011) present a qualitative comparative case study of consumer inclusion mechanisms in water tariff setting across three Western European utilities representing distinct regulatory archetypes: Vitens in the Netherlands (self-regulation), Agbar/EMA in Barcelona, Spain (bipartite negotiation) and Scottish Water/WICS in Scotland (independent regulation). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study demonstrates clear aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative comparative approach (Q2: Yes), a coherent analytical framework adapted from Stern & Holder (1999) across 15 transparency, participation and accountability indicators (Q3: Yes), and a nuanced presentation of findings that distinguishes formal legal provisions from practical barriers (Q9: Yes). However, methodological transparency for the primary interview component is weak (4 'Can't tell' items and 1 'No' item): informant sample sizes, recruitment procedures, interview protocols, ethical safeguards and qualitative coding/triangulation rules for assigning ordinal L/M/H scores are omitted from the published article (Q4, Q5, Q7, Q8: Can't tell), and researcher reflexivity is absent despite first-author affiliation with Vitens Evides International, funding from Suez Environment and acknowledged guidance from Agbar staff (Q6: No). Cross-case causal attribution is also inherently constrained by national legal-historical confounding across n=3 single-jurisdiction cases and by measuring procedural mechanisms rather than downstream tariff or service outcomes.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate concern (4 Can't tell / 1 No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative qualitative case study (three regulatory regime cases combining key-informant interviews and legal/regulatory documentary analysis)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research design and data collection notes in [PDF Page 4 of 13] Research design & Footnotes 1-2 (pp. 461-462); case selection and descriptive utility metrics in [PDF Pages 4-5 of 13] Description of the selected cases, Tables 1-2 (pp. 462-463); institutional/legal analysis and comparative ordinal ratings in [PDF Pages 5-10 of 13] The tariff setting processes & Application of regulatory governance principles, Table 3 (pp. 463-468); methodological limitations and future research in [PDF Pages 10-11 of 13] Discussion & Conclusion (pp. 468-469); author affiliations and funding in [PDF Page 1 of 13] (p. 459) and [PDF Page 11 of 13] Acknowledgements (p. 469).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is a primary qualitative comparative field and documentary case study that collects data through key-informant interviews (using a questionnaire with regulators, utilities, public authorities and consumer bodies) alongside secondary legal and regulatory document analysis across three purposively selected water pricing regimes, aiming explicitly at analytical rather than statistical generalization. The CASP Qualitative Checklist directly covers primary qualitative interview and documentary/field case studies; quantitative checklists (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, JBI, MMAT) and AMSTAR 2 do not apply because there is no quantitative sample estimation, quasi-experimental counterfactual or systematic literature search.
